articles.title: American-made goods also got more expensive under Trump tariffs, new research finds
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Bank of New York research shows Trump tariffs added 2.9 percentage points to consumer goods inflation through February 2026.
articles.body: Americans aren't just seeing the price tag increase for imported goods. Thanks to President Donald Trump's tariffs, they are now paying more for products made in the U.S.A., according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. In fact, the research finds that prices for many everyday goods would have fallen last year and into early 2026 without Trump's tariffs. The findings offer new evidence of how the sweeping tariff policy, a centerpiece of the president's economic agenda during his second term, have affected Americans’ wallets — and it's only getting worse with just one month until the midterm elections. TRUMP BET TARIFFS WOULD BRING BACK AMERICAN FACTORY JOBS. NEW REPORT SAYS IT DIDN'T WORK Economists had long warned that tariffs would drive up consumer prices, but measuring their precise impact has been difficult as trade policies shifted and companies made decisions about whether to absorb higher costs or pass them along to shoppers. Put simply, the New York Fed found that tariffs kept prices higher on many of the goods Americans buy every day. Without the tariffs, prices across the consumer goods examined for this study would have fallen by early 2026. Instead, they rose. The researchers estimated that tariffs added about 2.9 percentage points to prices across the goods they studied. And the impact, notably, was not limited to imported products facing the most fallout from tariffs. The New York Fed found that Trump's policies pushed up prices on American-made goods. Researchers estimated that about two-thirds of the tariff-related price increase came from imports, while roughly one-third came from products made in the United States. The White House pushed back, arguing that tariffs will ultimately benefit U.S. workers and be paid by foreign exporters. "President Trump’s America First trade agenda is reshaping the international economic order to reduce our trade deficit, revitalize American manufacturing, and deliver lasting benefits to our workers, farmers and producers," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital. The administration has maintained that foreign exporters reliant on access to the U.S. market will ultimately bear the cost of tariffs, Rogers added. A MUST-WIN MIDTERM STATE IS THE REAL LOSER OF TRUMP'S CANADA TRADE WAR Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute, told Fox News Digital that consumers may not see significant relief as long as tariffs remain in place. "What we know is that the tariffs have increased prices a bit," Lincicome said. "What we don't know is whether the prices will stay where they are or go up even a little bit more as companies finally cave and start passing on more of the tariff costs onto consumers." "As long as the tariffs remain in place, it's unlikely we're going to see price declines," he added. The research also found that tariff-related price increases can take up to a year to fully reach consumers, particularly when American manufacturers face higher costs for imported materials and components. Although the researchers estimate that the inflationary impact of existing tariffs has largely peaked, they expect consumer goods prices to remain higher than they otherwise would have been. 5 STATES COULD BE THE BIGGEST LOSERS IN TRUMP'S TRADE WAR WITH CANADA, EXPERT WARNS The findings could carry political implications as Trump and Republicans face voters in November after campaigning on lowering the cost of living. "When you campaign on lowering prices, and then you actually actively increase prices, it's probably gonna hurt when voters go back to the polls and are mad about prices still being too high," Lincicome said. Meanwhile, higher energy costs are adding another layer of pressure on American households. "It's really a double whammy for American consumers because first you had the tariffs which increased the prices of a lot of products. And then you had energy prices spike because of the Iran war," Lincicome said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He warned that rising diesel costs could push prices higher beyond the gas pump, increasing transportation expenses for businesses that rely on trucks, trains and agricultural equipment. "Those things are going to act as kind of another tariff because they're gonna increase the cost of getting that product to you," he said.

articles.title: The Iran war's unexpected impact on US defenses against China threat downplayed by top Army leader
articles.summary: Gen. Ronald Clark says China's PLA continues preparing despite Trump-Xi diplomacy as U.S. Army Pacific expands deterrence across the Indo-Pacific.
articles.body: Amid growing concerns that the Iran war is drawing away critical U.S. defenses from China's doorstep, the Army's top commander in the Pacific says the forces are using this unexpected opportunity to modernize. Gen. Ronald Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific, provided his assessment that diverting Patriot missile defenses to the Iran war has not increased risk to forces in the Indo-Pacific despite concerns about deployments impacting America's readiness for potential conflict with China. "Actually, it's given us an opportunity to modernize our systems here," Clark told Fox News Digital during a small-group interview at the Association of the United States Army's annual conference in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. Patriot systems have been redeployed from the Indo-Pacific to support operations in the Middle East, while U.S. forces in South Korea have also sent Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors to the region. An October Congressional Research Service report cited estimates that U.S. forces had expended roughly 1,700 Patriot and 200 THAAD interceptors during the conflict, while the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the military had used between half and two-thirds of certain interceptor inventories. The Pentagon's inspector general has cited strategic inventory shortfalls and manufacturing bottlenecks stemming from the conflict, raising questions about how quickly the U.S. could replenish its defenses in the event of another major confrontation. Clark said the deployments are giving Patriot crews firsthand experience defending against enemy attacks, while equipment upgrades are expanding what individual batteries can accomplish. He said an upgraded Patriot battery can now provide coverage that previously required an entire battalion, though he did not specify whether he was referring to geographic coverage or the number of threats the system can engage. Asked whether recent diplomatic progress between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping had changed his assessment of the threat from China, Clark said he believes the People's Liberation Army (PLA) is continuing its build-up. "Well, I believe they're continuing to prepare," Clark said. XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT The assessment comes weeks after Trump welcomed Xi to Washington for a high-profile state visit that produced new trade agreements and commitments to improve military communications. But the diplomatic progress has not resolved tensions over Taiwan and China's growing military reach across the Indo-Pacific, where American commanders continue preparing for a potential conflict. Clark did not say whether China's military preparations had accelerated or whether diplomatic outreach had changed Beijing's intentions. He emphasized that the U.S. military's responsibility is to remain ready for a potential conflict while working to prevent one. TAIWAN ANALYSTS SAY TRUMP-XI SUMMIT PRODUCED NO POLICY SHIFT BUT REAL TEST LIES AHEAD "Hopefully my legacy in this job is that when we walk away from command of USARPAC, that the deterrent posture of our command is such that we have not just prevented war, but we're preventing war in the future," Clark said. Clark said Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, recently discussed reviving disaster-management exchanges between the U.S. Army and China's PLA during talks with his Chinese counterpart. The exchanges would provide an opportunity for American and Chinese military personnel to work together on disaster response, restoring a channel of direct engagement that Clark said he hoped to see revived. "If you're able to have a conversation with your adversaries, you're able to share information with them in a way that makes them not want to fight," Clark said. He said U.S. Army Pacific would be responsible for coordinating the exchanges with its Chinese counterparts if the effort moves forward. He did not announce a date or say that Beijing had formally agreed to resume the program. The U.S. and Chinese militaries have periodically conducted disaster-management exchanges in the past, including an event hosted by the Army at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state in 2017. "The cost of going to war is just so high that it's our duty to, one, be absolutely prepared for that eventuality, but two, to prevent that from happening," Clark said. The diplomatic outreach comes amid continued confrontations between Chinese and Philippine forces in the South China Sea. As Fox News Digital previously reported, the Philippines tracked 101 Chinese navy and coast guard vessels around disputed waters in September, nearly double the number recorded in August. More recently, Philippine authorities accused Chinese forces of obstructing maritime operations and carrying out dangerous maneuvers near Philippine aircraft. CHINESE MILITARY ACTIVITY NEARLY DOUBLES AROUND KEY US ALLY IN DISPUTED WATERS Meanwhile, the Army has been expanding its capabilities across the Indo-Pacific, positioning additional forces and equipment closer to potential flashpoints as part of its effort to deter Chinese aggression. Clark said the Army now has more resources committed to the region than at any previous point in his career, including additional divisions, a corps headquarters and specialized formations designed to conduct long-range strikes and operations across multiple domains. "The Army is now better resourced in the Pacific than I've ever seen it," he said. He pointed to the Army's growing ability to support naval and air operations, including land-based weapons capable of striking targets at sea. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Clark said recent military war games have demonstrated the importance of those capabilities, including one maritime scenario in which the addition of Army forces changed an unfavorable outcome. "It's really tied to existing capabilities we have," Clark said, citing the Army's ability to detect targets, conduct strikes, protect military assets and sustain operations from land.

articles.title: Mamdani, City Council move to end iconic NYC horse-drawn carriage industry as workers face uncertain future
articles.summary: Romanch's Law would phase out Central Park horse-drawn carriages by 2028, but Mayor Zohran Mamdani's transition plan guarantees no financial payouts.
articles.body: New York City's iconic horse-drawn carriages could disappear from Central Park under an agreement reached Tuesday between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and City Council speaker Julie Menin, setting the stage for a vote to eliminate the historic industry. The agreement would ban horse-drawn carriage operations beginning June 1, 2028, if approved by the City Council on Oct. 22, ending a longtime tourist attraction amid concerns over animal welfare and public safety. The proposed legislation, known as Romanch's Law — named after 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who suffered fatal injuries in a horse-drawn carriage crash in June — would require city officials to develop a transition plan for carriage drivers, owners and stable workers, though financial compensation would not be guaranteed. MAMDANI'S LATEST FREEBIE SETS OFF ONLINE FURY AS CRITICS RIP CITY PRIORITIES: 'OPERA SOCIALISM' "The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected, and the horses are safe," Mamdani wrote on X. Animal rights group PETA celebrated the agreement after years of campaigning against the carriage industry. "This is long overdue, and it can't come quickly enough," PETA representative Ashley Byrne told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview Tuesday. Byrne cited incidents involving horses collapsing in city streets and colliding with vehicles, and said more than 70% of New Yorkers support a ban, a figure Fox News Digital has not independently verified. MAMDANI, NYPD GIVE SECURITY UPDATE AHEAD OF JEWISH HIGH HOLY DAYS, 9/11 25TH ANNIVERSARY The Central Park Conservancy also welcomed the agreement, emphasizing public safety. "We applaud the City Council for finally taking on this issue. For the Central Park Conservancy, this has always been a matter of public safety. We hope carriages can be phased out efficiently and humanely so that no one else ever suffers the fate of Romanch Mahajan," Conservancy President and CEO Betsy Smith said. But the Transport Workers Union sharply criticized the agreement, accusing city leaders of failing to provide meaningful financial protections for workers and carriage owners. "Council Speaker Menin's bill has no meaningful economic relief for workers," TWU International President John Samuelsen said in a statement. "It only says the city should prepare a worker transition plan by April 2027 and include weak measures like job fairs and job counseling." Samuelsen also accused Menin of exploiting the June death of 18-year-old tourist Romanch Mahajan to advance the ban. MAMDANI'S 'THIS IS ONLY THE BEGINNING' ANNOUNCEMENT CRACKING DOWN ON FOOD DELIVERY TIPS SPARKS OUTRAGE "Council Speaker Menin used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis. This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families' livelihoods are being destroyed," he said. Under the legislation, city agencies would have until April 1, 2027, to develop a workforce transition plan that includes job placement, career counseling, training and referrals to other transportation and tourism jobs. Officials would also have to consider compensation for carriage owners and assistance with retiring horses, but no payouts are guaranteed. "We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all," City Hall spokesperson Sneha Choudhary said. Fox News Digital reached out to Transport Workers Union Local 100, which represents carriage drivers and owners, for comment. Menin, who would be the first sitting City Council speaker to support the legislation, according to the Council, said the city must balance tradition with public safety and workers' livelihoods. "We can honor our city's traditions while recognizing when it's time to move forward in the interest of public safety, protecting workers, and strengthening our city's economic vitality," Menin said. The legislation follows the June death of Mahajan, a tourist from India who suffered fatal injuries after a horse-drawn carriage bolted, collided with another carriage and overturned in Central Park. "The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable," Menin said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Central Park Conservancy previously reported that the fatal crash was the eighth horse-related incident in or around the park in approximately 13 months. Days earlier, a carriage horse named Deniz reportedly collapsed and died while pulling tourists. Following Mahajan's death, TWU Local 100 called for tougher driver examinations, enhanced training and additional safety regulations rather than an outright ban.Mamdani's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

articles.title: Battleground Republicans break with Trump on key issues in final midterm sprint
articles.summary: Battleground Republicans like Mike Lawler and Jen Kiggans are touting bipartisan credentials and conflict with Trump as midterm elections near.
articles.body: Battleground Republicans are breaking from President Donald Trump with increasing frequency as Election Day draws closer and the party fights to protect its congressional majorities. With just three weeks until voters head to the polls to decide who controls Congress for the latter half of Trump’s term, some Republicans are putting distance between themselves and Trump as the party faces significant political headwinds. Veteran GOP strategist Doug Heye told Fox News Digital that such a strategy at this juncture was "not a surprise." "It happens in midterms when presidents aren’t popular," Heye said. "Add to that the more outlandish things he’s done — often on things that have nothing to do with lowering costs, ending the war with Iran, etc. — this was bound to happen." TRUMP VANISHES FROM GOP SENATOR'S CAMPAIGN WEBSITE AS POLL NUMBERS PLUNGE WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION It’s a similar situation to what’s played out with past presidents during a midterm election year, most recently with former President Joe Biden in 2022. And the Republican National Committee (RNC) is arguing that the party is united behind Trump, while conceding that GOP candidates have individual stakes. "Unlike the Democrats who are in a full-blown civil war with extremists, Republicans remain united behind the president's agenda of cutting taxes, lowering drug costs and securing our communities. We are laser-focused on winning, and our candidates will run the races necessary to best represent their districts and prevent Democrats from taking control," RNC spokeswoman Natalie Baldessarre said. And running their own races is what several are notably doing, balancing individuality with their support for Trump and the GOP base. At least two House Republicans, Reps. Jen Kiggans, R-Va., and Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., have touted conflict with Trump in advertisements. TRUMP-LINKED SUPER PAC PULLS FUNDING FROM 2 HOUSE REPUBLICANS AS GOP FIGHTS TO KEEP MAJORITY Kiggans is out with a new ad touting herself as "one of the most bipartisan members of Congress," who has taken on her "own party to protect jobs, and working with Democrats to save healthcare." One visual referenced a news article that said, "Kiggans bucks Trump on offshore wind." Meanwhile, Lawler recently released an advertisement in which he highlighted taking on "the left and the right," followed by a clip of Trump calling him a "pain in the a--" on state and local tax deduction issues. But for many, like Lawler, it’s a balancing act of trying to keep Trump and the GOP base happy, while courting independent voters. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said, "No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement, and the president understands how to communicate with them." "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," Ingle told Fox News Digital. "The president signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, lowered the cost of prescription drugs, sealed the border, drove violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, unleashed an energy revolution, added more than a million private-sector jobs and sent Americans’ 401(k)s climbing to record highs," Ingle continued. "The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction." Still, the political tightrope was on full display when Lawler appeared on stage at Trump’s midterm convention in September, when he noted he and the president didn't "always agree." He told Fox News Digital at the convention, "I fundamentally believe if you want to get things done, you have to be able to work with whoever the president is. And it's why I've consistently been rated among the most bipartisan and effective members of Congress." Former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., and Sen. John Husted, R-Ohio, also notably appeared at Trump’s convention in Dallas. They have, however, split from Trump on some key issues in an effort to show daylight between themselves and the president. CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? GOP BETS ON TRUMP AT HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION They have called for an end to the Iran war and have diverged from Trump on data centers — the president declared on Truth Social shortly after the midterm convention that "the only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor." But it’s a key sticking point for several Republicans on the trail who recognize the bad optics the hulking, windowless behemoths have with voters. Many, including Husted and Rogers, don’t believe it’s an issue that the federal government should have total dominion over. "What we've said is there should be a moratorium until we get all of the voters' decisions and questions answered," Rogers told Fox News Digital during the convention. "These are big decisions. I don't think there should be a federal ban, because if the federal government can ban it, it can also tell you have to have one." Another vulnerable GOP lawmaker who broke from Trump on the issue of data centers is Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Mich., who has maintained that it should be a decision for local governments whether to allow such facilities in their backyards. "When you have people colluding with these corporations to come in and build a data center, before people in the community even know about it, because of these non-disclosure agreements, I think that violates the trust that people have or don't have with their local officials right now," Barrett said on Fox News’ "The Big Weekend Show." Barrett is also one of a small handful of House Republicans who has consistently voted against the U.S. operation in Iran without congressional approval. The Middle East conflict has gained a steady stream of GOP opposition the longer it’s gone on, as evidenced by the growing number of Republicans voting for Democrats’ war powers resolutions in the House. Among them is Rep. Marianette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, who previously voted with the GOP on similar measures until the most recent such vote in mid-September. And Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, who voted against reining in Trump on Iran, noted on the Woo & WayCo podcast last week, "We need to get out of this war quickly." "What [Trump] did to stop a nuclear danger is a beautiful thing, but right now, you know, I don’t think anyone can cut a deal with Iranians, because you can’t trust them," Miller said. The Ohio Republican’s re-election chances are up in the air amid a slew of domestic abuse allegations from his ex-wife and former father-in-law. He did notably appear at Trump’s rally in Youngstown, Ohio. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Trump’s plan to import foreign beef has also gotten some pushback from vulnerable House Republicans like Miller-Meeks and Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa. Nunn, another battleground Iowan, introduced a bipartisan bill last month that would suspend Trump’s plan while directing the federal government to find a strategy to grow domestic cattle numbers. And some candidates, like Rep. Tom Kean, R-N.J., do not mention the president on their websites at all. References to Republicans on Kean’s site are few and far between, but it touts him as an "independent leader standing up for what is right for New Jersey." A separate White House official argued that Republicans distancing themselves from Trump "could not be further from the truth — President Trump is still the unequivocal leader of the Republican Party."

articles.title: Bipartisan senators demand Trump scrap Russia diesel deal, call it 'betrayal' of US allies
articles.summary: A bipartisan group of United States senators joined together in a letter pressuring President Donald Trump to nix the diesel deal with Russia.
articles.body: A bipartisan group of senators is urging Donald Trump to scrap his recently announced diesel deal with Russia, warning it could help President Vladimir Putin finance his war against Ukraine and calling the agreement "a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies." "The Treasury Department’s General License No. 135, which lifts sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports, only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians. Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," the senators asserted in the missive. The letter, which also includes a note of cc to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is signed by GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, Susan Collins of Maine, Alan Stuart Armstrong of Oklahoma, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and John Cornyn of Texas, as well as Democratic Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Dick Durbin of Illinois, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Chris Coons of Delaware. REPUBLICAN LAWMAKERS BREAK WITH TRUMP ON DIESEL DEAL WITH RUSSIA "We also recognize the urgent need to lower energy costs for American families and address the disruptions caused by the war with Iran. However, allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans. It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea. It will also endanger servicemembers operating overseas in support of Operation Epic Fury," the senators declared in their message. "Putin is a tyrant. Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. Maintain our legacy – and the duty America holds – as leader of the free world," they urged. TRUMP RUSSIA DEAL COULD FUEL PUTIN'S WAR, EX-NATO COMMANDER WARNS AS ZELENSKYY SAYS 'NYET' When asked during a gaggle on Tuesday whether he had been told that Russia would not utilize diesel money for bombs to use against Ukraine, Trump said no one "told me anything. That's a diesel deal not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us. That's a diesel deal that's gonna be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices," he said. "But they're not releasing that to us, they're releasing it to the entire world." The senators' message to the president comes after Trump, in a Truth Social post on Friday, announced, "I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel. TRUMP SAYS RUSSIA HAS AGREED TO DELIVER MILLIONS IN DIESEL FUEL AFTER 'HIGHLY SUCCESSFUL DISCUSSION' CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority. This is a very big and important announcement. Additionally, it must be understood, that Iran will not have a Nuclear Weapon!" the president declared in the post.

articles.title: Encuesta del CIS: el PSOE sube en intención de voto y supera en 12 puntos al PP
articles.standfirst: El Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas publica el barómetro de octubre
articles.summary: El Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas publica el barómetro de octubre
articles.body: El último barómetro del Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS) sitúa al PSOE como primera formación en intención de voto, con el 34 por ciento, 12 puntos por encima del Partido Popular, con un 22,2 por ciento. VOX sería la tercera fuerza política con un 17,1 por ciento. Los socialistas ganan un 3 por ciento respecto al barómetro anterior, mientras que el PP pierde un 3,3. En cuanto a los resultados de Sumar (6,1 por ciento) que plantea el barómetro de octubre, el organismo que dirige José Félix Tezanos aclara que la cifra corresponde a los grupos que firmaron la coalición de izquierdas, dejando fuera de este cálculo a Podemos. La formación de Irene Montero aglutina, según el CIS, un 3,1 por ciento en intención de voto y ERC, un 3 por ciento. La encuesta del CIS, realizada entre los días 1 y 6 de octubre, es especialmente relevante para palpar la opinión de la ciudadanía de cara a las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre. El estudio se ha realizado después del desahucio de Maricarmen, la mujer de 87 años cuyo caso impulsó movilizaciones ciudadanas. La acampada de Sol, en Madrid, es la más mediática y relevante. El acceso a la vivienda se ha convertido, tras este episodio, en parte central de la agenda electoral de las distintas formaciones políticas en España. La fórmula con la que los partidos de izquierda, al margen del PSOE, se presentarán a las próximas elecciones generales todavía no está clara. Por un lado, Frente Amplio ha designado a Ada Colau, exalcaldesa de Barcelona, como su candidata. Por otro, Podemos y ERC han sellado un acuerdo de colaboración para que Irene Montero y Gabriel Rufián hagan campaña juntos a nivel estatal. Ninguno de los dos bloques ha cerrado completamente la puerta a alcanzar acuerdos antes de los comicios del 29N.

articles.title: Congress can make real progress on preventing fraud in the lame duck
articles.summary: With the federal government’s annual deficit reaching $2 trillion in 2026, three bipartisan House-passed anti-fraud bills are currently awaiting Senate action during the lame duck session.
articles.body:
The fiscal year has closed, and the federal government’s annual budget deficit totaled $2 trillion in 2026 . To put this otherwise incomprehensible sum into perspective: Washington spent roughly $15,000 per household more than it collected in revenue over the past 12 months.

The $2 trillion deficit isn’t the result of a national emergency or temporary circumstance. It’s the nation’s current fiscal program. Washington is expected to average $2.4 trillion in annual deficits over the next ten years.

While only a lame duck session remains in the 119th Congress, the House of Representatives has already sent several bills to the Senate that could deliver substantial taxpayer savings by helping agencies prevent fraud in federal spending programs, a problem that the Government Accountability Office estimates costs the federal government between $233 billion and $521 billion annually .

The Pre-Payment Fraud Prevention and Treasury Data Access Act , sponsored by Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), would enhance the Treasury Department’s Do Not Pay system by adding new data sources and helping agencies verify eligibility before payments are made. The bill passed the Committee by a vote of 35-1 and passed the House with the two-thirds vote required under suspension of the rules.

The cleverly-named Zeroing Out Monetary Benefits Improperly Expended Act (or ZOMBIE Act), sponsored by Rep. Gary Palmer (R-Ala.), would update the federal law aimed to prevent improper payments by shifting the focus from backward-looking audits to real-time auditing and risk management. The bill would also require an annual convening — bringing state government officials to meet with the Treasury secretary and OMB director — to coordinate fraud prevention in state-administered programs. The bill passed the Committee 40-0 and the whole House by voice vote.

The Fraud Prevention and Accountability Act sponsored by Rep. Pete Sessions (R-Texas), would establish a permanent government-wide anti-fraud Inspector General for Fraud, Accountability, and Recovery within the Treasury Department. This would involve transferring the Pandemic Response Accountability Committee’s data analytics tools (including its promising AI-enabled Fraud Prevention Engine that can review thousands of applications per second) and capacities into a new inspector general and expand their mission. It would also strengthen the Treasury Department’s authorities to use Do Not Pay and other screening tools to vet payments in federal and state-administered spending programs. This bill passed the House by a vote of 240-181 with 28 Democrats supporting it.

Each of these bills is awaiting action in the Senate. With broad bipartisan support in the House, Senate leaders have an opportunity to hotline the bills when lawmakers return. Alternatively, a senator could bring the bills to the floor and seek their passage by unanimous consent. Which senator would be willing to publicly object to bipartisan reforms that simply strengthen the government’s tools for preventing billions of taxpayer dollars from being stolen by fraudsters?

To be sure, there’s much more Congress could do to increase government efficiency and prevent fraud. The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office has already laid out a broader agenda for improving government efficiency and preventing fraud, including a list of “ nine ways Congress can combat fraud in the federal government .” By its own estimate, its recommendations to federal agencies and matters for congressional consideration could produce between $132 billion and $251 billion in financial benefits .

Nobody should pretend that anti-fraud legislation will solve a $2 trillion deficit. But the enormity of the fiscal problem is not an argument against pursuing achievable savings. Rather, it is an argument for taking every reasonable opportunity to do so.

Senate leaders should make passage of bipartisan anti-fraud reforms a priority when lawmakers return for the lame duck session.

Dan Lips is a senior fellow with the Foundation for American Innovation.

articles.title: Iowa Senate candidates face off amid flurry of debates
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ A busy debate night ▪ Guilfoyle resigns ▪ Zacharia’s rocky start ▪ Trump adds more red state stops Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D) went head-to-head for the second and final time Tuesday night, just as early in-person voting is set to start in the battleground. Iowans…
articles.body:
Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D) went head-to-head for the second and final time Tuesday night, just as early in-person voting is set to start in the battleground.

Iowans are able to cast their ballots at county elections offices and some other locations beginning today, with the toss-up contest for retiring Sen. Joni Ernst ’s (R) seat at the top of the ticket. Nexstar affiliate WHO 13 in Des Moines hosted last night’s debate, focusing on issues like affordability and the Iran war. Nexstar also owns The Hill.

In one of the most notable moments of the night, Hinson broke with President Trump on the diesel deal that he made with Russia to import 300,000 tons of the fuel to the U.S. and global marketplace.

“We need to lower gas prices in this country. We need to lower diesel prices, but I don’t think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it,” Hinson said.

Trump’s announcement has spurred backlash from across the political aisle, including from those who say it amounts to supporting Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and violates federal law. More on that later.

Hinson said high energy costs should be addressed by temporarily lowering the gas tax, looking into a possible diesel rebate program for producers and investing in the U.S.’s biofuels.

Turek responded that this is a rare issue where the candidates agreed . Other parts of the debate weren’t so amicable.

Turek continued his attacks on Hinson over her growing wealth while serving in Congress, in particular her husband’s 2021 sale of his insurance agency to a private equity company. Hinson responded that she doesn’t own any publicly traded stocks and accused Turek of distracting from his own liabilities.

“His lies are beneath him on this race, and he’s muddying the water because he does not want to talk about his own liberal record here,” she said.

Hinson went after Turek for the number of floor votes in the Iowa state House that he missed. Turek acknowledged missing many of the votes but pointed to a busy campaign schedule, saying he’s been meeting with Iowans all over the state.

The Hill’s Caroline Vakil has a rundown of what else you need to know from the debate.

The Iowa showdown was one of about a dozen congressional or gubernatorial debates across the country last night.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) and Rep. Mike Collins (R) also met for a second time. Arguably the most notable moment concerned Ossoff’s political future if he holds on to win another term in the Senate.

Ossoff has increasingly been the subject of speculation about 2028 ambitions as his stock has risen within Democratic circles, but he pledged on stage to serve a full six-year term if he wins reelection.

“I have zero interest in running for president. I’m not running for president. I’m running for re-election to the Senate,” he said.

Ossoff has repeatedly denied interest in a White House bid, but that hasn’t quelled the talk. If he were to run, he wouldn’t be the first candidate to do so after ruling out a bid.

That club includes former President Obama , whose rhetorical style has been compared to the young senator. Obama said he wouldn’t run in 2006 before changing course for the 2008 election.

Collins rejected Ossoff’s denial, insisting “he’s running for president.”

Sen. Susan Collins (R) and former state Senate President Troy Jackson (D) found some common ground, just as the Iowa candidates did. Both candidates rejected the president’s tariff war with Canada, saying it’s harming Americans.

They also mostly agreed on the need for guardrails on AI data centers. Collins mentioned her support for the Ratepayer Protection Act, which advocates for the high energy costs associated with the centers to be mitigated. Jackson said he supports either the federal government or the state of Maine implementing more regulations.

Collins responded that it “sounds like Troy and I, oddly enough, are not that far apart on this issue.”

There was plenty of jousting as well in the third of give debates planned in the race.

Jackson continued his strategy of tying Collins to Trump, accusing her of not doing enough to end the Iran war and overturn the president’s tariffs. Collins noted her support for a war powers resolution, though she previously opposed it, and argued she was able to get some items removed from the tariff list.

Affordability has consistently been rated as the top issue on voters’ minds this cycle, regardless of the state.

An exclusive NewsNation/Decision Desk HQ poll released Tuesday found an overwhelming majority of voters believe current members of Congress are out of touch with their constituents’ spending habits. Insiders can read more about the poll’s findings here to learn more about how the public is viewing their economic concerns before they head to the polls.

▪ The Hill : 3 takeaways as Collins, Jackson duke it out.

A federal judge extended his block on the president’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, keeping it in place while the legal challenge plays out. He rejected the administration’s rationale that national security concerns were behind the move.

Pope Leo XIV had the lower lobe of his right lung removed after doctors discovered that the nodule on the lung was cancerous , the Vatican said. A release states that the surgery was successful and had no complications.

The head of the United Kingdom’s MI5 spy agency said Iran is trying to strike military sites in Britain, going beyond the traditional targets of dissident Iranians. He said the suspected plot to attack a U.S.-operated military base in the country is “not unique.”

Kimberly Guilfoyle speaks as President Trump listens at a reception celebrating Greek Independence Day in the East Room of the White House, March 24, 2025, in Washington. (Jacquelyn Martin, Associated Press file)

GREEK DRAMA: U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned Tuesday amid mounting scandals following a request from the White House , including a report that said she asked a Republican donor to send her $100,000 to pay off her American Express credit card.

“She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading,” Trump told reporters about Guilfoyle.

Trump also sought to distance himself from Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to Donald Trump Jr.

“She wasn’t a member of my family. I guess she dated my son a long time ago,” Trump said.

Guilfoyle confirmed in a social media post that her time as ambassador was “coming to an end” but pushed back against the allegations, which she said are false: “I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”

She also vowed to remain a “loyal supporter” of the president and his MAGA movement.

Guilfoyle was reportedly already under investigation by the State Department’s inspector general’s (IG) office. The top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), said the IG probe should continue and that Congress should conduct its own oversight, writing on social platform X , “resigning does not shield her from accountability.”

▪ The Hill : Guilfoyle scandal proves too much for Trump with midterms looming.

▪ The Hill : GOP donor says he’ll sue Guilfoyle, attorneys.

▪ The Hill : Rubio grapples with Greek drama surrounding Guilfoyle.

SETTING THE BAR : White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is facing a bombardment of questions and criticism following her first press briefing Tuesday.

Zacharia gave only a 14-minute briefing and took questions from three outlets. She broke the news that the administration had asked Guilfoyle to resign, but she wrapped up soon after. The Hill’s Julia Manchester reports that critics quickly noted Zacharia appeared visibly nervous during her briefing.

Zacharia raised eyebrows later in the day when she was asked where she passed her bar exam. Trump had described her as an attorney in his Truth Social post announcing her appointment.

A reporter asked Trump what state Zacharia passed the exam in, and she responded, “When I moved to China.” She later told NewsNation that she practiced international transaction law “with all the appropriate credentials.”

Her LinkedIn profile shows she has a J.D. from Pepperdine University and worked as an associate at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-2013.

▪ The Hill : Anthony Scaramucci says ‘clock is running’ on Zacharia’s tenure.

BANK ON IT : Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) is fundraising off the federal investigation and raid on her home that agents carried out Monday.

“Stand with Ilhan Omar,” a fundraising email reads, according to a screenshot obtained by The Hill’s partner network, NewsNation. “Donald Trump and DHS [Department of Homeland Security] have opened a baseless, partisan investigation into Ilhan Omar, and she needs us by her side as they escalate their attacks.”

Omar and fellow Democrats have denounced the investigation into the congresswoman as political, especially with less than a month to go before Election Day, breaking with Justice Department norms against taking public action in an investigation so close to an election.

White House border czar Tom Homan confirmed last month that Omar was under investigation but didn’t share further details.

▪ Fox News : Jeanine Pirro says office is investigating Omar’s financial disclosures.

▪ The Hill : David Axelrod questions timing of raid weeks before election.

TICKING UP : The number of GOP senators pushing back on the president’s deal to import millions of tons of diesel from Russia is growing.

Six Republican senators on Tuesday signed a bipartisan letter urging Trump to abandon the deal, which they said would have little impact on energy costs in the U.S. and would help Russian President Vladimir Putin in his war against Ukraine.

“It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance security cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea,” they wrote.

The Republican senators are Thom Tillis (N.C.), John Cornyn (Texas), Mitch McConnell (Ky.), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), Susan Collins (Maine) and Alan Armstrong (Okla.).

TAG TEAM : Liberal Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor and conservative Justice Neil Gorsuch joined together Tuesday to denounce “serious constitutional problems” in the federal government’s prosecution of a Mexican national for illegally reentering the country.

The court declined to hear an appeal from Jesus Herrera-Salazar , who challenged his deportation on the grounds that he was convicted on illegal entry twice. Sotomayor and Gorsuch agreed the court shouldn’t take the case since Herrera-Salazar had already been deported, but they cautioned that the facts of the case run into double jeopardy concerns.

“Should circumstances like these arise again, I encourage courts to avoid the constitutional absurdity that occurred here and give the Double Jeopardy Clause its full weight and meaning,” Sotomayor said in her opinion, which Gorsuch joined.

The president will travel to Bullhead City, Ariz., to deliver remarks at 4 p.m. EDT. He will then travel to Kalispell, Mont., for remarks at 8:15 p.m. EDT. He will then return to the White House.

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) speaks as Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., appears before the Senate Finance Committee, on Capitol Hill in Washington, Sept. 4, 2025. (Mark Schiefelbein, Associated Press)

MIDTERM BLITZ : Trump is adding more stops to his red-state tour as the GOP tries to shore up key seats to hold on to control of Congress or at least limit the Democratic margin of victory.

The president is heading to Montana today for a rally to boost GOP congressional candidate Aaron Flint , who is running for an open seat in the state’s 1st Congressional District. Flint is favored to win the seat against Democrat Sam Forstag , but Decision Desk HQ gives the challenger a 29 percent chance of winning.

The trip is the latest in a red-state blitz that Trump has seen Trump visit Oklahoma, Alabama, Alaska and Texas on three occasions. He’s also visiting states seen as more obvious battlegrounds this year, such as Arizona and North Carolina.

Trump is starting his day with a stop in Arizona, where Rep. Andy Biggs (R-Ariz.) is trying to oust Gov. Katie Hobbs (D).

He’s following that up with a visit to solidly Republican Kentucky this weekend to support congressional candidate Ed Gallrein in a district that has voted Republican for the House since 2002. Gallrein ousted Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has at times been a thorn in Trump’s side, in a primary earlier this year.

The Republican National Committee announced Tuesday that Trump will travel to Kansas next week as Sen. Roger Marshall (R) attempts to fend off an unexpected challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton . Democrats haven’t won a Senate seat in ruby-red Kansas since the 1930s.

Marchall is facing scrutiny following a report that he sued hundreds of patients for unpaid medical bills during his time practicing medicine. Trump defended Marshall in a lengthy Truth Social post, claiming he was legally obligated to pursue the debts.

“If he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the Law, and subject to criminal liability and arrest,” he said.

No federal or state law requires doctors to sue over unpaid medical expenses.

CLOSING TIME: Cornell University is suspending all fraternity parties through the end of the academic year amid the fallout from the Jane Doe lawsuit around an alleged gang rape in 2024 at the Chi Phi fraternity.

University president Michael Kotlikoff announced the move in a schoolwide message yesterday, saying any fraternity that violates the new rule will be placed on immediate suspension.

He also said the school would work with New York State Police to let their “experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators, who are independent of Cornell University” investigate allegations. Crimes that occur on campus are typically investigated by the campus police force, which has the authority of a law enforcement agency but is controlled by Cornell.

The school’s president announced several additional steps Cornell plans to take to address concerns about sexual assault on campus and the way the school and the local law enforcement handle those incidents going forward.

The school will appoint a dedicated case manager to help students navigate the process of reporting sexual misconduct, and it will add additional staff to its civil rights office. Kotlikoff also said Cornell will enhance existing bystander education and accelerate recommendations from the Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault.

Kotlikoff acknowledged culture problems on campus extent beyond Greek life.

“Research has shown that campus sexual assault is not limited to the fraternity system. At its core is the specific context of social behavior and a deeply disturbing prevalence of alcohol and drug abuse. While this is not a problem unique to Cornell, we are committed to setting a higher standard for education, oversight, and enforcement of safe social behavior and citizenship,” Kotlikoff wrote in his message.

articles.title: New York governor debate heats up as Blakeman, Hochul spar over Trump, sanctuary status, ICE shooting
articles.summary: The New York gubernatorial race heated up Tuesday as Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman clashed on the debate stage.
articles.body: The New York gubernatorial race heated up Tuesday as Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman clashed on the debate stage, with the pair trading jabs over President Donald Trump, a recent ICE-involved shooting and inflation. The debate opened with the candidates being asked about the conduct of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which last week drew outrage in New York City following the shooting of a 28-year-old Dominican national whom the Department of Homeland Security said refused to comply with lawful orders during a targeted operation in the Bronx. A 5-year-old boy inside Oscar Bergal's vehicle was unharmed. "Kathy Hochul appealed to ICE to let this criminal out. The question that New Yorkers have to ask is what was this guy doing in New York in the first place? It's because Kathy Hochul has made us a sanctuary state," said Blakeman, a Republican. "Think about it. This guy came into the country illegally. He's been convicted of a crime. He's got pending charges for dealing drugs, poison to our children. And he's a gangbanger. This is who Kathy Hochul is defending?" Blakeman continued. "I have a cooperative agreement with ICE until Kathy Hochul said we could no longer cooperate with ICE. We got over 2,000 illegal migrants out of my county with criminal records ranging from rape, attempted murder, robbery, burglary, drug dealing, carjacking, gang activity. And that's because we cooperated with ICE, and we didn't raid one school, one hospital, one daycare center or one church. If you cooperate with federal law enforcement, it makes for a safer community. That's what I did. Kathy Hochul is taking that ability away from us. That's why things like this happen." Hochul called Blakeman's response a "non-answer," because "he refused to condemn what ICE did." "So he basically says in the state of New York, he'd be fine if ICE agents shoot into cars, shoot guns into vehicles, not knowing who's inside and could have killed a 5-year-old child. If that doesn't shock the conscience of everybody — and it should shock his conscience as well — that he says, that's OK, that's how ICE is supposed to do it," Hochul added. "I'll tell you what. I oversee over 500 policing agencies in the state of New York, over half a million arrests every year. That's not how you conduct yourself. ICE is out of control. It's out of control in Nassau County." Blakeman pushed back, saying, "it never would have happened" but for Hochul's "sanctuary policy." "You have invited criminals to come into our state and prey on our communities. And now you won't let local law enforcement cooperate with ICE in an orderly way, like we did in my county," Blakeman added. "We didn't have any incidents in my county because we were allowed to cooperate with local law enforcement. But you took that tool away. The reason why that happened is because of you, Kathy Hochul, and your immigration policies, where you actually invite people into our state, give them free everything, and you don't care whether they're criminals or not. That's a bad policy." As part of her rebuttal, Hochul said, "I have a right to answer this one because this is so absurd. I have said, from the president on down, I said, New York is not a sanctuary for criminals, not a sanctuary for criminals. Full stop." The two candidates also clashed over Trump and the state of the U.S. economy. "He promised to cut energy costs. He promised to cut down grocery costs. And you know what? Everything has happened under your friend, Donald Trump, who you are the president of the fan club for Donald Trump. It's absurd how adoring you are of him. My gosh," Hochul told Blakeman. "Well, what he has done is raise gasoline prices and energy prices and the cost of tariffs have driven up everything in the state. If you bought groceries lately, my God, the people are suffering. And that didn't have to be the case. Why are we at war with the rest of the world?" "You like to talk about Donald Trump all the time, because you don't want to talk about your record," Blakeman responded. "I'm talking about my record right now," Hochul said. "Because it's a record of misery and failure," Blakeman continued. "The highest taxes, utility rates that are 70% higher than the national average. But let me say something about Donald Trump. Donald Trump is my friend. He's endorsed me. But so is Bonnie Lautenberg, a liberal Democrat whose husband, Frank, served in the United States Senate and was a pillar of the Democratic Party. Actor Debra Messing, who is a liberal Democrat who supports me because she trusts me to make safer communities, improve the quality of life here in New York." "Alright, you got two votes," Hochul said. "Good for you."

articles.title: Trump says 'we are looking into' other Dan Sullivan on Alaska ballot, warns about governor's race
articles.summary: President Donald Trump tells Fox News that Dave Bronson, a Republican running for governor, should drop out after falling to his preferred candidate in the GOP primary.
articles.body: President Donald Trump says federal authorities are "looking into" Dan Sullivan, an independent challenger who goes by the same name as the Republican incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, in the Alaska Senate race. Trump made the statement in an interview with Fox News after a campaign rally in Alaska on Tuesday night. He suggested the second Sullivan's presence in the race was a "hoax" by Democrats to siphon voters away from the Republican candidate. "We are looking, I can't say federal, but we are looking into it. It's a disgrace. We have, I call him the real Dan Sullivan, a great senator from Alaska. And in the race, they put somebody named Dan Sullivan who knows nothing about politics. His name happens to be Dan Sullivan. They even wanted to change his middle initial, which was different. They wanted to make it an S so that it could be exactly correct. I think it's just terrible that they did it," Trump said. SEEING DOUBLE: SECOND DAN SULLIVAN ADVANCES, SETTING UP BIZARRE ALASKA SENATE BALLOT "And actually, he got two points or something in the primary. The real Dan Sullivan won it, but ... It's a terrible thing. It's another hoax by the Democrats," he added. Trump also weighed in on the gubernatorial race in Alaska, where he has endorsed GOP candidate Bernadette Wilson. Other GOP candidates have been hangers-on in the race, despite Wilson winning the primary. Trump called on her Republican competitor, Dave Bronson, to drop out of the race. "He doesn't have to, but he should, because, frankly, he lost in the primary by substantial numbers to Bernadette. And I'm not involved that much in, you know, Alaska politics, other than I want to see Dan and Nick get in. But she won in the primaries, and the others should have dropped out. So now you have three Republicans running against one Democrat. And I don't like that. I don't like those odds very much. But there, she's great, and maybe she'll get in, but I thought I had an obligation to endorse her," Trump said. Trump went on to criticize the Democrat in the race, Mary Peltola, following her criticism that Sullivan had voted in favor of the war in Iran. "Can you imagine if they attacked our cities, and they attacked places where we are, including right here in Alaska? You would see turmoil far greater. We have a lot of oil flowing right now in the almost strait, we control it. The war is going to be over very, very soon. We're going to have a big victory very shortly. Very, very shortly, and oil is going to come way, way down. Gasoline is going to come down to where it was before," Trump said. So you're going to see it. But most importantly, Iran, the number-one state sponsor of terror, will never have a nuclear weapon. If they had one, you might not be standing here right now," he added.

articles.title: Cong defends crop insurance payouts, accuses BJP of misleading farmers
articles.summary: Congress defends Karnataka RWBCIS crop insurance payouts, says compensation is weather-index based and accuses BJP of misleading arecanut farmers on premiums.
articles.body: Mangaluru: District Congress Committee president Padmaraj R Poojary on Wednesday defended the state govt over crop insurance payouts under the Restructured Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme (RWBCIS), accusing local BJP functionaries of misleading farmers due to their alleged lack of understanding of the scheme.Addressing reporters, Poojary countered allegations by Belthangady BJP MLA Harish Poonja, who had blamed the Congress govt for reduced insurance compensation to growers. He termed the BJP's allegations baseless, stating that payouts were determined by scientific parameters and predetermined conditions specified in the scheme's term sheets, rather than the discretion of the state govt.“It is our misfortune that an elected representative lacks even the basic knowledge of where, whom, and when to criticise,” Poojary said, taking a dig at MLA Harish Poonja.Explaining the premium-sharing arrangement for arecanut, Poojary said the total premium is 35%, of which farmers contribute 5%, the Union govt 10% and the Karnataka govt the remaining 20%.He clarified that compensation under RWBCIS is calculated based on weather indices recorded by automated weather stations operated by the Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Centre (KSNDMC).
